disclaimer: Original unvalidated discussion exercise based on public safety guidance; not a recalled or official examination item, clinical protocol or validated scoring instrument. Not for patient care. Confirm current local guidance and supervision arrangements.
title: New type 2 diabetes: shared priorities and a sustainable care plan
setting: A fictional supervised Australian general practice with access to diabetes education and multidisciplinary referrals. Treatment decisions require the full clinical record and current local guidance.
case: A 49-year-old person attends to discuss a recent diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. They feel overwhelmed, work irregular hours, support relatives at home and are unsure what the diagnosis means. A friend has suggested an expensive restrictive diet. The person asks for one plan that will work immediately. They have not yet had a comprehensive diabetes assessment in this practice. Present how you would establish priorities, assess immediate needs and begin a collaborative care plan.
prompts: How would you first check for symptoms requiring urgent assessment and establish what the patient understands and most wants help with?
What clinical history, medicines, risk factors and baseline complication assessment would you review before selecting an individualised management plan?
How would you explain the diagnosis and realistic care goals without blame, assumptions about diet or culture, or a promise of immediate cure?
How would you agree a manageable initial plan, explore affordability and literacy barriers and involve appropriate diabetes, pharmacy or allied-health support?
How would you check understanding, arrange follow-up and explain which changes or symptoms should prompt earlier medical advice?
reflection_rubric: Checks immediate clinical safety before treating the encounter only as routine education; recognises the need for a comprehensive clinical record and assessment.
Explores the patient's goals, work and family circumstances, understanding, medicines and barriers, and uses person-centred rather than judgemental communication.
Individualises goals and review priorities, including relevant cardiovascular, renal, eye, foot and other complication risks, without inventing results or giving an unsupported medication regimen.
Offers achievable education and multidisciplinary support, discusses the practicality of proposed lifestyle changes and avoids endorsing an expensive diet without appropriate evidence and context.
Uses teach-back or equivalent checking of understanding, documents agreed responsibilities and arranges continuity and a clear follow-up plan.
source_notes: Uses the reviewed RACGP type 2 diabetes handbook introduction: care should respond to the person's preferences, needs and values; education and ongoing review are part of care. The handbook contains complication-specific sections, but this station supplies no treatment doses, universal targets or claims that one diet suits everyone.
